zebralogic.title: Interpret adjacency and ordering clues correctly
zebralogic.principle: When a clue describes a spatial relationship (e.g., "X is somewhere left of Y" or "X is directly left of Y"), enforce the appropriate positional constraint: use a strict inequality for "somewhere" and an exact offset of one for "directly left/right".
zebralogic.when_to_apply: Whenever a clue mentions left/right positioning, adjacency, or ordering between two entities.
zebralogic.example: Treating "directly left of" as merely "somewhere left of", allowing extra houses between them.

zebralogic.title: Interpret distance clues correctly
zebralogic.principle: When a clue says "N houses between X and Y", enforce that exactly N houses separate them, i.e., the absolute position difference is N + 1.
zebralogic.when_to_apply: Whenever a clue mentions a specific number of houses between two items.
zebralogic.example: Interpreting "one house between X and Y" as a distance of 1 instead of 2.

zebralogic.title: Treat 'somewhere left/right of' as inequality
zebralogic.principle: Clues that say "X is somewhere left/right of Y" impose only a strict ordering (pos(X) < pos(Y) or pos(X) > pos(Y)) without requiring adjacency.
zebralogic.when_to_apply: When a clue uses the phrase "somewhere left of" or "somewhere right of".
zebralogic.example: Assuming "somewhere left of" means immediate left, thus incorrectly restricting positions.

zebralogic.title: Apply exclusion constraints
zebralogic.principle: When a clue explicitly forbids an attribute from a particular house or forbids two attributes from co‑occurring, enforce that exclusion by removing those possibilities from the candidate sets.
zebralogic.when_to_apply: When a clue contains "not" or "cannot" statements.
zebralogic.example: Allowing Bob to be placed in house 6 despite the clue "Bob is not in the sixth house".

zebralogic.title: Enforce uniqueness across each attribute category
zebralogic.principle: Each value in a category must appear exactly once across all houses; after assigning a value, remove it from the candidate sets of other houses in the same category.
zebralogic.when_to_apply: Throughout the solving process, after any assignment.
zebralogic.example: Assigning the same child name to two different houses.

zebralogic.title: Preserve original case of attribute values
zebralogic.principle: When outputting the final grid, copy each attribute value exactly as it appears in the problem statement, preserving capitalization and spelling.
zebralogic.example: Changing "high school" to "High School" in the output.

zebralogic.title: Make forced assignments when only one candidate remains
zebralogic.principle: If after applying all constraints a house (or an attribute) has exactly one possible remaining value, assign it immediately.
zebralogic.when_to_apply: During constraint propagation, whenever a domain reduces to a single option.
zebralogic.example: Leaving a house with two possible names when only one is viable, missing a forced assignment.

zebralogic.title: Disambiguate overlapping attribute values using clue context
zebralogic.principle: When a word could belong to multiple attribute categories, use surrounding words in the clue to determine the correct category.
zebralogic.when_to_apply: When parsing clues that contain ambiguous terms.
zebralogic.example: Treating "Alice" as a child name when the clue actually refers to the person named Alice.

zebralogic.title: Interpret 'next to each other' as adjacency
zebralogic.principle: When a clue states that X and Y are "next to each other", enforce that they occupy immediately neighboring houses (|pos(X) - pos(Y)| = 1).
zebralogic.when_to_apply: When a clue uses the phrase "next to each other" or "adjacent".
zebralogic.example: Treating "next to each other" as a non‑adjacent ordering, allowing a house in between.

zebralogic.title: Bidirectional equivalence for name-attribute clues
zebralogic.principle: When a clue directly links a specific name to an attribute (e.g., "Carol is the person with a high school diploma" or "Alice is the person who loves swimming"), enforce a two‑way binding: the name and the attribute must be assigned to the same house, and the attribute cannot appear with any other name.
zebralogic.when_to_apply: Whenever a clue states that a particular person (by name) has a specific attribute.
zebralogic.example: Assigning high school to Bob while also assigning high school to Carol, ignoring that "Carol is the person with a high school diploma" forces high school to be paired only with Carol.

zebralogic.description: Interpreting 'N houses between' as distance N
zebralogic.why_it_happens: The model treats the phrase as a direct positional offset, forgetting that 'N houses between' means there are N houses separating the two, i.e., a distance of N + 1.
zebralogic.how_to_avoid: Convert 'N houses between X and Y' into the constraint |pos(X) - pos(Y)| = N + 1.

zebralogic.description: Ignoring equivalence clues that bind two attributes to the same house
zebralogic.why_it_happens: The model often records a one‑way implication instead of a two‑way binding, allowing the bound attribute to appear elsewhere.
zebralogic.how_to_avoid: Treat every equivalence clue as a bidirectional constraint and remove the bound values from all other candidates.

zebralogic.why_it_happens: The model may forget to enforce that each attribute value appears exactly once, leading to duplicate assignments.
zebralogic.how_to_avoid: After each assignment, delete that value from the domains of all other houses in the same category.

zebralogic.description: Altering attribute values (spelling/casing) instead of copying them verbatim
zebralogic.why_it_happens: The model normalises text during generation, changing capitalisation or spelling.
zebralogic.how_to_avoid: Store the original strings and output them unchanged in the final grid.
